4.text: The winter sleeping-room serves also for only a single small family.

5.text: Sometimes two inner rooms are joined together at an angle. There is no

6.text: partition between, and a separate lamp is lighted by each family in its own

7.text: part. This large double sleeping-room is quite similar to that of the Maritime

8.text: Chukchee and Asiatic Eskimo, as will be described later. In my opinion,

9.text: the stationary winter house is the typical form of the Chukchee dwelling,

10.text: while the movable tent is a variety comparatively new, and not even very

11.text: well adapted to the exigencies for which it is used. It is cumbersome, and

12.text: requires many reindeer to carry it, especially when compared to the Lamut

13.text: tent. When under way, it hampers considerably the progress of a Chuk-

15.text: Summer House. — The summer habitation is arranged in about the same

16.text: way as the movable winter tent, except that its place cannot be changed

17.text: till the first snow is on the ground. Therefore all the sledges are piled

18.text: together for the summer. The best driving-sledges are untied, and the lashings

19.text: and wooden parts carefully gathered in bundles and concealed in the middle

21.text: The whole is protected with parts of old tent-covers not in use. These

22.text: generally serve as tarpaulins. For the summer tent and for the summer

23.text: sleeping-room, old worn-out covers are used, and the people also wear old

24.text: clothing which was discarded in winter. The sleeping-room cover is closely

25.text: cropped with a sharp knife, and is usually put up with the hair side out. A

26.text: large piece of tent-cover tarpaulin is stretched over it above, resting on several

27.text: sticks fastened to the outer frame. This serves to keep off the rain, which

28.text: would come through the vent-hole and through the small holes of the outer tent.

29.text: The place of the camp cannot be changed during the whole summer;

30.text: but in the middle of June, in connection with the first summer ceremonial,

31.text: the tents are broken up and shifted some fifty or sixty feet. This change

32.text: is very desirable, because the house is exceedingly unclean. Sometimes at

33.text: the end of July the family will again change to avoid the offensive smell of

34.text: their old surroundings. Even in winter the people are often driven out of

40.text: and the scraping of skins — are done in this lodge. In its simple conical

41.text: shape, it occurs also among the Russianized Yukaghir as a summer dwelling

42.text: or as a dog-shelter. Long logs that are collected for fuel in winter are
